title: Snowball Earth
description: Worldwide glaciation episodes during the Proterozoic eon
wiki_lead:
The Snowball Earth is a geohistorical hypothesis proposing that during one or more of Earth's icehouse climates, the planet's surface was nearly entirely frozen, with little or no liquid water exposed. This global glaciation hypothesis is most commonly associated with the Cryogenian Period, which included two major glacial episodes: the Sturtian (c. 717–660 Ma) and Marinoan (c. 650–635 Ma).
Proponents of the hypothesis argue that it best explains sedimentary deposits that are generally believed to be of glacial origin at tropical palaeolatitudes and other enigmatic features in the geological record. Opponents of the hypothesis contest the geological evidence for global glaciation and the geophysical feasibility of an ice- or slush-covered ocean, 
and they emphasize the difficulty of escaping an all-frozen condition. Several unanswered questions remain, including whether Earth was a full "snowball" or a "slushball" with a thin equatorial band of open (or seasonally open) water. The Snowball Earth episodes are proposed to have occurred before the sudden radiations of multicellular bioforms known as the Avalon and Cambrian explosions; the most recent Snowball episode may have triggered the evolution of multicellularity.

History


First evidence for ancient glaciation
Long before the idea of a global glaciation was first proposed, a series of discoveries occurred that accumulated evidence for ancient Precambrian glaciations. The first of these discoveries was published in 1871 by J. Thomson, who found ancient glacier-reworked material (tillite) in Islay, Scotland. Similar findings followed in Australia (1884) and India (1887). A fourth and very illustrative finding, which came to be known as "Reusch's Moraine", was reported by Hans Reusch in northern Norway in 1891. Many other findings followed, but their understanding was hampered by the rejection (at the time) of continental drift.


Global glaciation proposed
Douglas Mawson, an Australian geologist and Antarctic explorer, spent much of his career studying the stratigraphy of the Neoproterozoic in South Australia, where he identified thick and extensive glacial sediments. As a result, late in his career, he speculated about the possibility of global glaciation.
Mawson's ideas of global glaciation, however, were based on the mistaken assumption that the geographic position of Australia, and those of other continents where low-latitude glacial deposits are found, have remained constant through time. With the advancement of the continental drift hypothesis, and eventually plate tectonic theory, came an easier explanation for the glaciogenic sediments—they were deposited at a time when the continents were at higher latitudes.

grok_lead: Snowball Earth is a geological hypothesis proposing that Earth underwent extreme global glaciations during the Cryogenian Period of the Neoproterozoic Era, approximately 720 to 635 million years ago, when ice sheets covered nearly the entire planet from pole to equator, with only possible refugia of open water at the equator in some models, though recent research suggests limited open ocean areas persisted in tropical regions during certain intervals. These episodes, primarily the Sturtian (about 717â660 million years ago) and Marinoan (about 650â635 million years ago) glaciations, are thought to have lasted for millions of years each, dramatically altering Earth's climate, ocean chemistry, and biosphere. The hypothesis was first proposed by Joseph Kirschvink in the early 1990s and gained prominence through work by Paul F. Hoffman and colleagues, who linked it to enigmatic geological features observed worldwide. Key evidence includes glacial deposits such as tillites and dropstones found at low paleolatitudes (near the equator), indicating ice reached tropical regions, as documented in formations like the Rapitan Group in Canada and the Chuos Formation in Namibia. Overlying these glacial layers are distinctive cap carbonates âthick sequences of limestone and dolomite deposited rapidly after deglaciation âsuggesting a sudden shift to warm, COâ-rich conditions that precipitated global ocean chemistry changes. Additionally, the resumption of banded iron formations (BIFs) during these periods points to anoxic, iron-rich deep oceans beneath the ice, as oxygen levels were low due to suppressed photosynthesis. Initiation mechanisms for Snowball Earth likely involved a combination of factors, including the supercontinent Rodinia's configuration with large landmasses at low latitudes, enhancing silicate weathering that drew down atmospheric COâ and weakened the greenhouse effect; this was exacerbated by a fainter young Sun (about 6% dimmer than today) and possibly large asteroid impacts or methanogen die-offs reducing greenhouse gases. Termination occurred through persistent volcanic outgassing, which built up COâ under the insulating ice sheet until a critical threshold triggered rapid melting, leading to the cap carbonate deposition and a potential hothouse rebound. Biotically, these events may have driven evolutionary bottlenecks, nearly extinguishing early life but possibly spurring the diversification of multicellular organisms post-glaciation, linking to the Ediacaran biota and subsequent Cambrian Explosion. Despite strong support, the hypothesis faces debates: some evidence suggests "slushball" scenarios with partial open oceans allowing refugia for life, rather than a fully frozen planet, and questions persist about the exact duration, synchrony, and global extent of the glaciations, with recent studies, including 2026 research on sedimentary varves, using isotopic, magnetic, molecular fossil, and sedimentary data refining low-latitude ice evidence and elucidating life survival in meltwater refugia. Overall, Snowball Earth exemplifies how extreme climate feedbacks could reshape planetary habitability.
